transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-14 09:30 PDT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel, Chris Nguyen, Daniel Ross (Redwood); Samir Rao, Elena Torres, Ben Cho (Aperture Health)

Summary:
Weekly POC check-in focused on Dedicated sizing, autoscale policies, and burst gating behavior observed in last weekend's soak. Agreed actions to run controlled stress in staging, tweak reserve buffer and eviction thresholds, and finalize pricing for pilot committed capacity. Discussed security questions (SOC2/KMS) and network egress considerations for VPC private deployment.

Topics:
- Observed latency and eviction events from 2027-09-12 soak
- Autoscale policy tuning (scale-up thresholds, cooldowns, max-burst)
- Burst buffer sizing and reserve eviction policy
- KV cache prefixing and cold-start impact
- Security docs and pilot commercial terms

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do quick status and then get into the burst gating stuff, chris you wanna kick off with the data?
[00:28] Chris: yeah I can, um so from the weekend soak we saw two eviction windows where requests hit the reserve and we had fallback to the small hosted model, so p95 shot from 160ms to 420ms, p99 to 980ms, and token unit cost increased about 28 percent because of the fallbacks and replays
[01:05] Samir: sorry can you repeat the bit about the fallback, was that because the dedicated pool dropped nodes or because of the routing policy?
[01:17] Chris: good question, it's a mix — we had a transient GPU OOM on node pool, and the smart router tried to route to dedicated spare capacity but reserve was depleted, so it fell back to compatible hosted variant which increased cost and latency. there may be an orchestration quirk that evicted workloads earlier than expected
[01:45] Ben: and the eviction you're referring to is the reserve buffer eviction? like reserve tokens or sessions?
[01:52] Chris: reserve buffer, yes, we use reserve units tied to the dedicated replica group; when reserve goes below threshold our eviction policy frees low-priority sessions, that is when the router will attempt to fallback.
[02:15] Elena: i remember we had kv-cache cold starts during one of those windows, could that have multiplied latency?
[02:24] Chris: absolutely, cold kv cache plus model warm-up increases initial latency. we logged increased prefix-miss rates for the kv keys tied to user sessions. enabling prefix caching in staging decreased cold start p95 by about 30 percent in our internal runs
[02:50] Maya: okay actionable then — chris will flip prefix caching and increase reserve buffer for the staging run, samir will run the scheduled stress test. also quick commercial check, samir you mentioned you had a procurement timeline, remind us?
[03:08] Samir: timeline is still end of september, legal wants to vet SOC2 docs and a high level SSO/SAML flow; budget finalization dependent on pilot numbers we saw last week
[03:23] Daniel: we'll share SOC2 snapshot and a quick network egress note — if you're doing VPC peering we have guidance on egress cost controls and private endpoints
[03:36] Samir: perfect, also on the autoscale policy can we see the cooldown slightly longer, we saw flapping when we had aggressive scale down, it caused more churn and then evictions
[03:48] Chris: yep that aligns. current default is 60s cooldown, we can extend to 180s for the pilot and change the scale-down threshold to require sustained under-target for 3 minutes. that reduces thrash but increases reserved cost.
[04:10] Elena: what's the tradeoff on cost? like how do we reason about reserve vs pay-as-you-go?
[04:18] Maya: good question — dedicated reserved GPUs give predictable throughput; you pay monthly for the pool, burst buffer is an add-on. with aggressive autoscaling you save on reserved cost but risk higher tail latency and fallbacks which increase token cost. we gave an example in the deck: a 20 percent drop in reserved capacity with fallback increased token spend by ~30 percent in the soak.
[04:47] Ben: can we capture the token accounting with the staging run so we can compare?
[04:51] Chris: yes we'll export token-level logs and include routing tags so you can map tokens to model variant and fallback events
[05:05] Samir: on burst sizing, what's your recommended starting point?
[05:12] Chris: for your traffic shape (bursty peaks 5-10k rps for short windows) we recommend a burst buffer equal to 1.5x your expected peak qps converted to token throughput, so for you that's roughly a 3-gpu buffer for 30 minute bursts. but if you expect long peaks we recommend 4-6 gpu buffer or use dynamic burst with ramp policies
[05:40] Elena: hmm 3 GPUs sounds heavy for cost, is there an intermediate option like queued requests or degraded-mode outputs?
[05:48] Maya: yes you can use graceful degradation — e.g., prefer cached replies, reduce max tokens, or route heavy requests to quantized variants with slightly lower quality. we can configure a fallback tiering: dedicated -> quantized-dedicated -> hosted-compatible.
[06:08] Ben: does the platform support model variant priority? like pin high-priority routes to dedicated no matter what?
[06:16] Chris: yes per-route pinning exists; you can also set a hard SLA flag that prevents fallback for specified routes but then you'll see drops if capacity isn't available — we usually only use hard pin for 1-2 critical endpoints
[06:28] Samir: okay for the pilot we want critical inference pinned (PHI redaction) but other non-critical chat can fallback
[06:35] Chris: sounds reasonable. we'll show how to set route.Priority and SLA flags in the console during the handover doc
[06:44] Maya: moving to the runbook, i'll summarise — staging stress window, prefix caching on, reserve buffer increased to 3 GPUs, cooldown extended to 180s, token logging enabled. any concerns?
[06:57] Elena: just one — model warm up time is significant for our long-context models, can we pre-warm KV cache and keep a small warm pool?
[07:05] Chris: yes there is a warm pool option; we can keep a tiny warm replica for low-latency on first request. tradeoff is cost vs latency. for pilot we suggest 1 warm instance and the rest on-demand.
[07:22] Ben: about eviction strategy, when reserve hits threshold what gets evicted first?
[07:27] Chris: low-priority sessions, idle sessions, and sessions with low usage score. that said, we can modify the eviction ranking to prefer evicting long-tail large-token sessions first to minimize impact to active short requests
[07:45] Samir: are there metrics we can get to visualize eviction impact?
[07:49] Chris: yes we will provide a dashboard with eviction count, fallback rate, p50/p95/p99 per route, and cost per token over time
[07:58] Maya: quick pause — legal/security stuff? daniel you had something to share?
[08:04] Daniel: brief — SOC2 Type II attestation is available, we'll share the latest report redacted. for KMS we support customer-managed keys via the KMS integration; for on-prem you'll have HSM options in the private package. also SSO via SAML and OIDC, and we can do SCIM provisioning
[08:28] Samir: and about data residency, we need logs retained in-region for 12 months for compliance, is that doable?
[08:34] Daniel: yes we can keep audit logs in the EU or specific region, retention policy configurable; we'll include a sample config and what fields are stored
[08:44] Elena: is there anything about egress costs when peering to your dedicated VPC?
[08:49] Maya: egress costs depend on cloud region and whether you use private peering. we have a recommended setup with VPC endpoints that minimize cross-region traffic; daniel will share best practices
[08:59] Samir: ok next on the agenda is the pricing delta for the burst buffer — maya you mentioned you'd update the estimate?
[09:06] Maya: yes i'll update with two options: conservative (reserve + small burst buffer) and aggressive (reserve + larger burst + warm pool). we'll include expected monthly and burst-overage estimates.
[09:18] Ben: for the staging stress, what's the exact test we'll run?
[09:22] Chris: plan is: 60 minute window, step traffic every 5 minutes, ramp to peak of 8k rps for 10 minutes, hold, then back down. we'll collect p50/p95/p99, fallback count, eviction events, and token cost. Samir will trigger it and provide expected test user prefixes
[09:40] Samir: we'll do that Thursday 02:00 UTC as discussed. do you need any special access?
[09:45] Chris: need an IAM role for the staging cluster to pull logs and trigger scaling sim, and a temporary API key to run the traffic generator. we'll send a short checklist after the call.
[09:58] Maya: want to call out a small config caveat — if you opt into the dynamic burst ramp, there's a slightly higher risk of oscillation; we prefer manual pre-sized burst for the pilot
[10:13] Elena: ok manual pre-sized sounds fine for now, we'll evaluate dynamic after the pilot
[10:18] Ben: any competitor-specific intelligence we should know — we run some tests with other vendors last month — Anthropic's latency was good but cost higher, Lambda had issues at scale. just FYI
[10:30] Maya: useful context, thanks. we'll include a short benchmark note in the handover docs.
[10:38] Daniel: last thing — handover plan: after staging stress and logs verification we'll do a 1-hour joint readout and then you (aperture) can sign the pilot reserved commit if numbers look good
[10:50] Samir: sounds like plan. procurement wants an invoice template too, can you provide?
[10:55] Maya: yes we'll attach a pro-forma and the term sheet.
[11:02] Chris: ok i'll prep the staging config and run the preliminary internal check by tomorrow, maya will send runbook and pricing, daniel will share security docs
[11:12] Maya: great, thanks everyone. any final questions?
[11:17] Elena: not from me, thanks all
[11:19] Samir: thanks, talk soon
[11:22] Meeting end

Notes on transcript quality: auto transcription had several proper-name swaps (Aperture/Apertur), some timestamps approximate, and occasional dropped punctuation. Speaker labels sometimes generic, but content verified by Maya and Chris after call.
